doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Childhood Halloween gigs at bars and a fancy restaurant
summary: As kids he and his brother played blues at bars on Halloween for tips, until a maitre d' threw them out of an upscale restaurant with a nickel and two pennies.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Oh I will add one other anecdote, I’ll make you laugh. Okay? One of the — this is talking about getting outside the schools. When I was a young kid, my brother played clarinet and he played up through high school and then he became a police officer and detective and you know top, top, top cop. Anyway in those days you could do this, but my mom and aunts, depending on what year it was, would drive us around on Halloween to bars. And we would be in like a hobo outfit and we had this old hat that somebody got from the Salvation Army. Right? And we knew one tune which was basically a blues type thing [scats]. Okay? Right? Like Joe Avery’s blues. So we would go to these bars, and you know the drunks, “Hey look at these two little kids” and they would throw money you know. So believe me, in those days it was a lot of bucks. But one gig we go to what used to be a restaurant. It’s right around the corner from here and believe me every time I pass it I think of it, a really hoity toity restaurant. So you know my mother says, “Well why don’t you go in there, it’s a fancy place, there’s people that got a lot of money.” All right? So my brother and I open the door, we walk in and we just start playing. The maitre d takes the both of us by the scruff of our collar and escorts us not in a very polite way out and throws a nickel and two pennies at us and says, “Get the hell out of here.”
Well now I know what you made on your first gig.
Yeah, you know. But it’s important to get the kids out and playing. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-
